9                     UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT                           
10                   SOUTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA                          
11                                                                            
12  UNITED STATES OF AMERICA,           Case No.:  23-cv-541-LL-BJC           
13                            Plaintiff,  ORDER DENYING DEFENDANT             
                                       CITY OF SAN DIEGO’S MOTION            
14  v.                                                                        
                                       FOR LEAVE TO TAKE                     
15  CITY OF SAN DIEGO, et al.           ADDITIONAL DEPOSITIONS                
                                       [ECF No. 94]                          
16                          Defendants.                                       
17                                                                            
        Before the Court is Defendant City of San Diego’s (“City”) “Motion for Leave to 
18                                                                            
   Reopen Rule 30(B)(6) Depositions; Take Five Additional Individual Depositions; and 
19                                                                            
   Take One Additional Rule 30(B)(6) Deposition.”  ECF No. 94.  For the reasons set forth 
20                                                                            
   below, City’s motion is DENIED.                                           
21                                                                            
     I.   BACKGROUND                                                         
22                                                                            
        On October 2, 2024, the Court held a status conference with Plaintiff United States 
23                                                                            
   of America (“USA”) and City to address ongoing discovery disputes that the parties 
24                                                                            
   briefed in a status report filed on September 13, 2024.  See ECF Nos. 88, 92.  During the 
25                                                                            
   status conference, City requested the Court consider its request to retake several 30(b)(6) 
26                                                                            
   depositions  of  USA  employees  and  notice  additional  depositions  beyond  the  ten-
27                                                                            
   deposition limit set by Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(a)(2)(A)(i).  USA objected to City’s request and 
28                                                                            
1  noted that City only mentioned this request to USA a few days prior to the scheduled status 
2  conference with the Court.  At the conclusion of the status conference, the Court requested 
3  City submit briefing on these issues.  City submitted its briefing on October 10, 2024 (ECF 
4  No. 94), and USA filed its opposition on October 22, 2024.  ECF No. 98.   
5        In addition, the Court granted an extension on the fact discovery deadline twice per 
6  City’s request.  Specifically, the Scheduling Order initially set the fact discovery cutoff 
7  for August 7, 2024.  ECF No. 61.  Following a status conference held on August 5, 2024, 
8  the fact discovery deadline was extended to September 6, 2024.  ECF No. 78.  On 
9  September 13, 2024, the Court entered an order granting City’s motion to extend the 
10  discovery deadline, making the new fact discovery cutoff date November 6, 2024.  ECF 
11  No. 87.                                                                   
12    II.  DISCUSSION                                                         
13       A.   Reopening 30(b)(6) Depositions of Amy Jo Hill, Lonie Cyr, and Louis 
14       Cardinale                                                            
15       City moves to re-open three 30(b)(6) depositions and re-depose Amy Jo Hill, Lonie 
16  Cyr, and Louis Cardinale for two main reasons.  First, City of San Diego argues that USA 
17  failed to provide City with indices of documents reviewed by the deponents in sufficient 
18  time  to  facilitate  their  preparation  for  the  depositions.    See  ECF  No.  94  at  9 
19  (“Approximately sixty-seven (67) minutes before the deposition, USA’s counsel produced 
20  [an] ‘Index of documents reviewed by L. Cardinale”); Id. at 6 (“[t]wenty-four (24) minutes 
21  before the deposition, USA’s counsel transmitted to City’s counsel a list of seventy-three 
22  (73) documents reviewed by the witness.”).  Additionally, City claims that USA failed to 
23  “adequately prepare their witnesses to testify.”  See Id. at 1.           
24        Regarding  USA’s  timing  for  disclosure  of  documents  prior  to  its  30(b)(6) 
25  depositions, City attached a copy of its Deposition Notice that stated:   
26            “Under Fed. R. Civ. P. 34, the United States shall produce an   
             index to or a copy of each document that the witness relies on, or 
27                                                                            
             witnesses  rely on, in preparing to  testify  as  a Rule 30(b)(6) 
28            representative.  If  the  document  has  not  been  previously  
1            produced, the United States shall produce a copy of the document 
             rather than listing it in an index.”  ECF No. 94, Ex. 1 at p. 2.     
2                                                                            

3       Contrary to the City’s deposition notice, FRCP 34 does not require parties to 
4  provide an index of each document that a witness relies on, nor does it provide a certain 
5  timeframe for such action to take place prior to commencing a deposition.  See Burlington 
6  N. & Santa Fe Ry. v. United States Dist. Court, 408 F.3d 1142, 1147 (9th Cir. 2005) (“Rule 
7  34 requires that a written response to a discovery request be served within 30 days of the 
8  service of the request. The response must provide access to the information requested, 
9  either by permitting inspection or by producing documents”).              
10       City does not state that USA failed to produce documents in response to their 
11  document requests or even failed to provide the requested document index.  Rather City 
12  finds it unfair that USA provided (in some circumstances) a “bates-numbered” list of 
13  documents, did “not indicate which documents correspond to which [deposition topic] 
14  categories,” and did not provide City with the document indices well in advance of the 
15  depositions.  ECF No. 94 at 8.  USA is not required under Rule 34 to provide indices at 
16  all or within a certain timeframe.  The fact that the documents had already been provided 
17  to City indicates that USA satisfied the requirements of Rule 34.   As such, the Court does 
18  not find that the timing of USA providing City with the optional indices of documents 
19  used to prepare 30(b)(6) witnesses supports reopening depositions.        
20       Additionally,  City  alleges  that  USA  did  not  sufficiently  prepare  its  30(b)(6) 
21  witnesses to testify.  See e.g. ECF No. 94 at 4 (“Ms. Hill was unable to answer basic 
22  questions such as the names of individuals from City that were involved in the negotiation 
23  of the MOA with USA.”); Id.  at 7 (“Ms. Cyr stated in her testimony ‘[i]f you have a 
24  question about a particular document, we can open that up and look at it.’”); Id.  at 10 
25  (“Mr. Cardinale stated, ‘I can’t tell what these Bates numbers refer to.’”).   
26         Indeed, a 30(b)(6) deposition is not a “memory contest,” and an entity has a duty 
27  to “‘make a conscientious, good-faith effort to designate knowledgeable persons” and 
28  “prepare them to fully and invasively answer questions about a designated subject matter.”  
1  See Starline Windows Inc. v. Quanex Bldg. Prod. Corp., No. 15-CV-1282-L (WVG), 2016 
2  WL 4485564, at *4 (S.D. Cal. July 21, 2016).  Nothing in the record before the Court 
3  supports finding that USA’s witnesses failed to review documents or prepare for the 
4  depositions.  Here, the witnesses simply could not recall some specifics from his/her 
5  review  of  documents.    Having  previously  received  and  presumably  reviewed  the 
6  documents in question, City could have directed the witness to specific documents to 
7  refresh their recollections or given the witnesses an opportunity to locate documents 
8  related to City’s questions.  It is unclear whether City chose not to do so.  For these reasons, 
9  City’s request to reopen the 30(b)(6) depositions of Amy Jo Hill, Lonie Cyr, and Louis 
10  Cardinale is DENIED.                                                      
11       B.   Leave for City of San Diego to Take Five Additional Individual Witness 
12       Depositions                                                          
13       The City also requests the Court’s permission to take five additional individual 
14  witness depositions.  A party seeking to exceed the presumptive ten-deposition limit must 
15  establish good cause to do so.  Ocean Garden Prods. Inc. v. Blessings, Inc., No. CV-18-
16  00322-TUC-RM, 2020 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 18755, 2020 WL 570947, at *2 (D. Ariz. Feb. 
17  5, 2020).  Good cause is “a high standard that continues to rise with each request for 
18  additional depositions.”  Nevarez v. Forty Niners Football Co., LLC, No. 16-CV-07013-
19  LHK-SVK, 2018 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 182254, 2018 WL 5023370, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 16, 
20  2018).  Rule 30 directs that the Court “must grant leave” to take additional depositions to 
21  a party who has met this standard “to the extent consistent with Rule 26(b)(1) and (2)” of 
22  the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.  Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(a)(2).  See also Ocean Garden, 
23  2020 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 18755, 2020 WL 570947, at *2; Lloyd v. Valley Forge Life Ins. 
24  Co., No. C06-5325 FDB, 2007 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 40526, 2007 WL 906150, at *2 (W.D. 
25  Wash. Mar. 23, 2007).                                                     
26       Under  Rule  26(b)(1),  parties  may  discover  “any  nonprivileged  matter  that  is 
27  relevant to any party’s claim or defense and proportional to the needs of the case . . .”  
28  While Rule 26(b)(1) creates an expansive universe of discoverable information, Rule 
1  26(b)(2), in turn, places certain defined boundaries on that universe, by stating that the 
2  Court “must limit the frequency or extent of discovery otherwise allowed” if it determines 
3  that “(i) the discovery sought is unreasonably cumulative or duplicative, or can be obtained 
4  from some other source that is more convenient, less burdensome, or less expensive; [or] 
5  (ii) the party seeking discovery has had ample opportunity to obtain the information by 
6  discovery  in  the  action[.]”    Fed  R.  Civ.  P.  26(b)(2)(C)(i)-(ii)2  (emphasis  added).  
7  Therefore, if the Court finds that none of the grounds for limiting discovery outlined in 
8  Rule 26(b)(2) applies to Defendant’s request to conduct additional depositions, the Court 
9  must grant leave for the additional depositions.  On the other hand, the Court must deny 
10  the request if any of these grounds applies.                              
11       Here, the Court finds that both grounds for limiting discovery apply to City’s 
12  request to take additional depositions.  First, City has not established good cause to 
13  conduct an additional 30(b)(6) deposition or five additional witness depositions because 
14  City had ample opportunity to request additional depositions.  As noted above, the parties’ 
15  original fact discovery deadline was August 7, 2024.  ECF No. 61.  Prior to the initial fact 
16  discovery deadline, this Court held a status conference with the parties on August 5, 2024 
17  where the parties discussed outstanding discovery issues.  ECF No. 78.  Following the 
18  status conference, the parties filed two status reports: one on August 23, 2024 (ECF No. 
19  84) and one on September 13, 2024 (ECF No. 88).  Neither status report raised concerns 
20  about City needing to take more depositions beyond the ten allotted per FRCP 26.  Indeed, 
21  City did not mention this request until the status conference held on October 2, 2024.  ECF 
22  No. 92.  City waited to request permission to take additional depositions until 2 months 
23  after the initial fact discovery deadline and after receiving a three-month extension on the 
24  fact discovery deadline.  As such, allowing six additional depositions at this stage would 
25  be “highly burdensome” and would “divert employees away from normal duties to spend 
26  significant time preparing” for the additional depositions.  ECF No. 98 at 16.     
27       Second, City has not shown that good cause exists to take the additional depositions 
28  because the anticipated topics of the examinations are duplicative of prior discovery 
1  requests and/or depositions conducted.  City is requesting to take five additional witness 
2  depositions  all  relating  to  the  witnesses’  “knowledge  of  relevant  facts,  especially 
3  regarding the MOA which was executed in May of 2000.”  ECF No.  94 at 14.  City further 
4  states that it is necessary to depose these individuals since “the Navy rotated staff every 
5  couple of years” during the period in question for this litigation.  Id.  However, City 
6  already served a 30(b)(6) deposition notice and conducted an examination of Amy Jo Hill 
7  on the following topic: “Memorandum of Agreement By and Between the United States 
8  of America and City of San Diego for Economic Development Conveyance and Public 
9  Benefit Conveyances at the Former Naval Training Center, San Diego (MOA).”  ECF No. 
10  94, Ex. 1, at 2.  Since the topic of the additional inquiries has already been covered in a 
11  deposition,  the  requested  additional  witness  depositions  will  result  in  duplicative 
12  testimony.    Therefore,  City’s  request  to  take  five  additional  witness  depositions  is 
13  DENIED.                                                                   
14       C.   Leave for City of San Diego to Take Additional 30(b)(6) Deposition of 
15       USA                                                                  
16       City also requests permission to conduct an additional 30(b)(6) deposition on the 
17  following category: “The USA’s purchase, use, application, transport, storage, treatment, 
18  disposal or dumping at the NTC (including the Boat Channel) and/or MCRD from 1922 
19  to the present relating to the following chemicals: Perfluorinated compounds; Chromium 
20  (also known as Chrome; Chromium Element; Chromium Metal; Metallic Chromium; Cr; 
21  DLA05001; RTECS GB4200000; and all products that are or include Cr3 and Cr6); DDT; 
22  and Chlordane.”  ECF No. 94 at 10.  As articulated above, the Court finds that City’s delay 
23  in requesting this additional deposition topic weighs against granting the request.  City has 
24  contacted chambers several times since August of 2024 to raise numerous discovery 
25  disputes, but neglected to raise this issue until a status conference held on October 2, 2024.   
26       Additionally, the Court finds that an additional deposition on this topic would be 
27  duplicative of prior deposition topics.  Specifically, Topic No. 8 on City’s deposition 
28  notice, dated August 27, 2024, requests information related to contaminants found within 
1          Boat  Channel.   See  ECF  No.  94,  Ex.  1  at  pp.  4-5  (information  “regarding  the 
2    negotiation and the remediation of the NTC Boat Channel [including], but not limited to: 
3   ||the  selection of chemicals  of concern for analysis  and exclusion of other chemicals  of 
4   ||concern  from the  analysis”).   City’s  description  of Topic No.  8  was  broad  enough  to 
5    include the additional category listed above.  Indeed, City fails to aver that the requested 
6   ||category of an  additional  deposition would not be  cumulative  or duplicative  of topics 
7    raised in prior depositions.  As such, the Court DENIES City of San Diego’s request to 
8   ||conduct an additional 30(b)(6) deposition. 
9      Hl.   CONCLUSION 
10         For the reasons set forth above, the Court DENIES City of San Diego’s Motion for 
11   |;}Leave  to  Reopen  Rule  30(B)(6)  Depositions;   Take  Five  Additional  Individual 
12 || Depositions; and Take One Additional Rule 30(B)(6) Deposition.”  ECF No. 94. 
13 
14         IT IS SO ORDERED. 
15    Dated:  December 30, 2024
